summary: Sets out the compliance statements for the CMC certificate enrollment protocol, saying what an implementation must support to be considered compliant. The data structures and transports are covered in other documents; this one pulls together what is needed for interoperability. It was replaced by RFC 10004.

eli5.summary: This is the checklist a certificate-request program must tick to say it follows the rules properly. It has been replaced by a newer checklist, RFC 10004.

questions: what must a cmc implementation support
subtitle: The checklist of what a certificate-enrollment client, registration authority or CA must support to count as compliant CMC.

tldr.problem: The CMC certificate enrollment protocol is defined across several documents with many optional parts, so two implementations could both claim CMC and still fail to work together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5274 lists, for all entities and then for end entities, registration authorities and certification authorities, which message types, algorithms and controls MUST, SHOULD or MAY be supported.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 6402 and obsoleted by RFC 10004, so the current compliance rules live there.

today: RFC 5274 was updated by RFC 6402 and obsoleted by RFC 10004, so the current CMC compliance requirements are in the newer document.

sections.title: The CMC Roles
sections.content:
CMC (Certificate Management over CMS) works as a client/server relationship. In the simplest case the client is the End Entity (EE) asking for a certificate and the server is the Certification Authority (CA) that issues it.

A Registration Authority (RA) can sit in between. It acts as the server toward the requester and as the client toward the issuer, and any number of RAs can be chained this way. With several RAs, it is normal that not all of them see every request. This document does not cover specialised RAs, such as a key escrow agent.

The ASN.1 structures and transports are defined elsewhere, in RFC 5272 and RFC 5273. This document only says what a compliant implementation must do. Its requirements are split by role: all entities, servers, clients, EEs, RAs and CAs.
sections.eli5: Getting a digital ID is like ordering through a shop. You ask, maybe a helper passes your order along, and the issuer finally makes it. Each person in the chain has their own list of jobs.

sections.title: Requirements for All Entities
sections.content:
All compliance statements in the structure and transport documents (RFC 5272 and RFC 5273) still apply unless this document says otherwise. On top of that:

  • All entities MUST support Full PKI Requests, Simple PKI Responses and Full PKI Responses. Servers SHOULD support Simple PKI Requests.
  • All entities MUST support the CRMF syntax for certification requests. Servers SHOULD also support the PKCS #10 syntax.
  • The extendedFailInfo field SHOULD NOT be filled in; the failInfo field SHOULD be used instead.
  • All entities MUST implement the HTTP transport. Other transports MAY be implemented.
sections.eli5: Everybody must know the basic forms and how to send them over the web. Extra ways of sending are allowed but not needed.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
The algorithm rules mostly follow a pattern: one older algorithm is a MUST, a stronger one is a SHOULD.

  • Signatures: all entities MUST verify DSA-SHA1 and RSA-SHA1 signatures and MUST generate either DSA-SHA1 or RSA-SHA1. Verifying RSA-PSS with SHA-1, and SHA-256 with RSA and RSA-PSS, is strongly suggested.
  • Encryption: AES MUST be supported for content encryption, and RSA MUST be supported as a key transport algorithm. RSA-OAEP SHOULD be supported. An entity that supports key agreement MUST support Diffie-Hellman.
  • Passwords: an entity that supports PasswordRecipientInfo MUST support PBKDF2 for key derivation and AES key wrap. If AuthenticatedData is supported, PasswordRecipientInfo MUST be supported too.
  • Controls: for Identity Proof Version 2, POP Link Witness Version 2, Encrypted and Decrypted POP, and Publish Trust Anchors, SHA-1 and HMAC-SHA1 MUST be implemented, while SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256 SHOULD be.

EEs that generate Diffie-Hellman keys for certification MUST support Section 4 of RFC 2875 (Diffie-Hellman Proof-of-Possession). CAs and RAs that verify proof of possession MUST support Section 4 and SHOULD support Section 3.
sections.eli5: The rules name a secret-code method every program must know, plus a stronger one it should also know. It is like requiring everyone to know a basic lock and suggesting a better one.

sections.title: Controls and CRMF Restrictions
sections.content:
Table 1 lists each CMC control and the support level for EEs, RAs and CAs. Controls that all three roles MUST support include Extended CMC Status Info, Identity Proof Version 2, Identification, POP Link Random, POP Link Witness Version 2, Data Return, Transaction ID, Sender Nonce, Recipient Nonce, Query Pending and Confirm Certificate Acceptance.

Some differ by role. Revocation Request is a SHOULD for EEs and RAs but a MUST for CAs. POP Link Witness is a SHOULD for EEs but a MUST for RAs and CAs. Modify Cert Request, Batch Request, Batch Responses and Control Processed are N/A for EEs and MUST for RAs; CAs MUST implement them if designed to work with RAs. Get Certificate, Get CRL and Publication Information are optional.

Authenticate Data and Publish Trust Anchors are optional, but the RFC says strong consideration should be given to them, since they give a simple way to distribute trust anchors into clients without user intervention.

Section 4.3 also restricts CRMF. The registration control tokens id-regCtrl-regToken and id-regCtrl-authToken MUST NOT be used (the identification and identityProof controls do the job instead). id-regCtrl-pkiArchiveOptions SHOULD NOT be supported, and id-regCtrl-protocolEncrKey is not used.
sections.eli5: There is a big table saying which jobs each role must do, should do or may skip. A few old, unsafe tools are banned from use.

sections.title: Rules for End Entities, RAs and CAs
sections.content:
Clients and servers have no additional requirements beyond the common ones. The role-specific rules are:

  • EEs: an entity that implements Diffie-Hellman MUST implement either the DH-POP proof of possession from RFC 2875, Section 4, or the challenge-response controls id-cmc-encryptedPOP and id-cmc-decryptedPOP.
  • RAs: RAs SHOULD be able to do delegated proof of possession, and if so MUST implement id-cmc-lraPOPWitness. All RAs MUST implement promotion of id-aa-cmc-unsignedData.
  • CAs: working with RAs is strongly suggested, because it lets substantial administrative work move to an RA. CAs MUST make at least minimal checks on all public keys and MUST enforce proof-of-possession checking before issuing any certificate. They SHOULD check for known bad keys, such as small subgroups for DSA-SHA1 and DH keys, or known bad RSA exponents.

A CA MAY delegate proof of possession to an RA in three cases: a challenge/response pair must be used, an RA escrows the key and checks that way, or an unusual algorithm is validated at the RA.
sections.eli5: The issuer must always check that you really own the secret key you are asking an ID for. It may let a helper do that check in a few special cases.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document builds on RFC 5272 and RFC 5273 and includes their security sections by reference. It warns that knowing how an entity is expected to operate is vital for deciding which requirement sections apply, and that care is needed to implement the necessary code fully.

It also notes that cryptographic algorithms have been and will be broken or weakened. Implementers and users should check that the listed algorithms still make sense at their security level. The IETF may issue documents on the current state of the art; it names RFC 2785 and RFC 4270 as two examples.
sections.eli5: Secret-code methods can get cracked over time, so people must keep checking the ones they use are still strong enough.
